processing: Pan-fired, not steamed: fresh leaf is heated, turned and massaged in a pan, then dried. It is not allowed to oxidise, and it takes on a curly, rounded shape.
harvest_season: Little is documented for Takachiho alone; as with other Japanese green teas, spring is the main and most prized picking.
appearance_dry: Curly, rounded leaf in muted olive green.
appearance_liquor: Lighter and clearer than most green teas, a pale gold.
appearance_wet: Open olive-green leaf, as is typical of pan-fired tea.
taste_profile: Refreshing and aromatic, with a mouthfeel closer to some Chinese greens than to sencha, and the toasty note typical of pan-firing.

brewing.notes: Slightly hotter water than you would use for sencha. Hot water brings out the aroma, and the rounded leaf opens slowly, so give the first steep a full minute.

vintage_note: Usual for Japanese green tea: sold as the current year's harvest and best drunk fresh, within about a year. It comes in small batches from family farms, so stock can run out before the next spring. Producer names matter more than any vintage label.
description:
Takachiho-cha is the pan-fired green tea of the Takachiho area in the mountains of northern Miyazaki. Kamairicha makes up only about 1% of Japan's green tea, and it is made almost entirely here and in the surrounding Nishiusuki District.

Where most Japanese tea goes through a steamer, this leaf goes into a pan, where it is heated, turned and massaged. That leaves it curly and rounded and stops oxidation, so it is a true green and not a light oolong, despite the shape.

The cup is paler and clearer than sencha, fragrant and refreshing, with a texture that reminds many people of Chinese tea. The common mistake is brewing it cool like sencha: it wants slightly hotter water to wake the aroma.

Around 33 family-run farms keep it going, so buy by producer and check the harvest date. One of them, Kai Seicha-en, won an agriculture minister's award in 2015 for fragrance, a useful name to start with.
history:
Pan-fired tea has been an everyday drink in Takachiho for centuries, though no precise starting date is documented.

The farms remain small and family-run, and the labour-intensive method keeps output limited.
